opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't because I thought what Andreas was doing was wrong. I have a lot of respect for that direction, and I think a company is a great vehicle for certain kinds of problems, especially when you already know what you want to build and the main challenge is scaling it, engineering it, and getting it into people's hands.

But for me, "AI for AI," using AI to help us understand and improve AI itself, still feels like a research question, not an engineering question. I don't think we know the right abstractions yet. When I worked on things like Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, what excited me wasn't only the performance. It was the idea that a model could be interpretable enough to talk back to you, so a scientist could look inside and learn something. I want to push that idea further: can we build systems that help us discover the principles behind learning, not just produce bigger black boxes?

In a company, even a very good one, there's natural pressure toward what works now and what can ship. That's healthy for a company, but it makes it harder to spend a year on something that might look strange or useless at first. Many of the ideas I care about started out looking a bit naive, like asking whether we could treat neural networks the way physicists treat nature, finding the simple laws underneath the complexity.

There's also a personal side. I'm still at a stage where I want to follow my curiosity and be free to be wrong. If I join someone else's vision, I'd be optimizing their objective function. Right now I want to find out what my own objective function is. Maybe later these paths will converge, and I'd be very happy if they did. But at this point I felt I should try my own approach, even if it's riskier.

r001.rationale: He says he wants to follow his own curiosity, develop his own objective function, and try his own approach to AI for AI.

r002.rationale: He describes AI for AI as a research question and notes uncertainty about its principles, but does not clearly address how that research might become a commercial product.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that Andreas and I actually agree about the destination but disagree about the road.

When I was finishing my PhD at MIT with Max Tegmark, I spent a lot of time thinking about what "AI for science" or "AI for AI" should even mean. The dominant view in Silicon Valley, and I think Andreas largely shares it, is scaling: you build a very large, general model, you give it tools and agents, and you let it do research the way a human researcher would, just faster and in parallel. That's a perfectly reasonable bet. If it works, it works, and I don't think anyone should dismiss it.

But my own background is in physics, and physics has given me a different intuition. I'm interested in whether we can actually understand what these systems are doing, not just make them bigger. Work like KAN, the Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, came out of that itch. I wanted architectures where the learned structure is legible, where a scientist can look at a model and read off a formula or a mechanism. To me, "AI for AI" means using interpretability and the science of deep learning to design better AI, not only using AI as a labor force to run more experiments.

So when I thought about joining Andreas, the question I asked myself was: would I be able to pursue that scientific angle there, or would I be swept into the gravity of the main product? Startups have a center of mass, and rightly so. Andreas has a vision he needs to execute, and the people who join should be aligned with that execution. I respect that too much to be the person inside pulling in a different direction.

There was also a more personal reason. I'm still young in my research career, and I felt that if I didn't try my own ideas now, when the cost of being wrong is low, I'd regret it later. It's much easier to go from "I tried and it didn't work" to joining a bigger effort than the other way around. If my approach fails, that's genuinely useful information for the field, and I'll happily go collaborate. If it works, then we have a second path that's complementary to scaling rather than competing with it.

And I'd add that Andreas and I still talk. I don't see this as a rivalry. The field is big enough, and frankly the problem is hard enough, that we need people placing different bets. I just wanted mine to be the one that takes understanding seriously.

r001.rationale: He says he wanted to try his own ideas while early in his career and pursue his scientific angle through an independent path.

r002.rationale: The response discusses possible research outcomes and collaboration, but does not say he remained open about how to commercialize the research.

astra-6.text: For me, the appeal was having the freedom to explore my own ideas about AI for AI. Joining Andreas’s company would have meant committing to a shared direction, and I wanted to give my own approach a chance—to find out where it would lead and whether it would work.

r001.rationale: He says he wanted freedom to explore his own AI-for-AI ideas and give his own approach a chance, identifying that as his reason for pursuing his own path.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the main motivation was to have the freedom to explore my own ideas about AI for AI. Joining Andreas’s company would have been one way to work on that broader goal, but I wanted to find out where my own approach could lead. When you’re still figuring out the right questions, having the space to choose your direction—and change it—is really valuable. So it was less about deciding against his company and more about wanting to try this path myself.
